newsitem.title: CHINA: China says controversial punishment to stay.
newsitem.headline: China says controversial punishment to stay.

text.p: China on Sunday dismissed calls for the abolition of re-education through labour, an administrative punishment that human rights groups say has been increasingly used to remove dissidents from circulation without trial.
"Re-education through labour...can only be strengthened and cannot be weakened," the official Legal Daily said in a front-page commentary.

International human rights groups and Chinese dissidents have called for the abolition of re-education through labour, saying officials increasingly favour it as a way of removing dissidents from circulation without a complicated judicial process.
The Legal Daily defended the practice, saying it was needed to "maintain social peace and prevent and reduce crime".
It gives people suspected of committing petty crimes a chance to turn over a new leaf, the newspaper said.
Re-education through labour calls for police to care for charges "like parents treat their children, doctors treat their patients, and teachers treat their students", it said.
Chu Hailan, wife of veteran dissident Liu Nianchun, scoffed at the purported soft treatment of detainees.
"You must be joking ... They say it all the time but they never do it," Chu said in a telephone interview.
In May, Chu accused labour camp officials of torturing her husband with electric shocks and water deprivation after the activist went on a hunger strike to protest his imprisonment.

Liu is serving three years of re-education through labour at the Shuanghe labour camp in northeastern China's Heilongjiang province after he challenged the government by writing daring petitions demanding political reforms.

The Legal Daily trumpeted re-education through labour, saying some detainees have been admitted into universities while others have become selfless and are ready to "take up the cudgels for a just cause".
More than 2.5 million people have undergone re-education through labour since the administrative punishment was introduced in 1957, it said.
More than 280 labour camps across China hold about 230,000 detainees, the newspaper said.

Last week, Zhu Yaping, wife of dissident Yao Zhenxiang, filed a lawsuit against authorities in Shanghai for refusing to let her visit or exchange correspondence with her husband, who is serving three years of re-education through labour.
Yao, 37, fled to Hong Kong in 1994 and was granted political asylum in France. He returned to Shanghai in February 1996 after police promised not to arrest him.
Despite the promise, Yao and his brother were arrested in April last year and the dissident was accused of illegally leaving China and distributing pornographic material.

International human rights groups and Western governments have criticised Beijing for a wide-ranging crackdown on dissent in 1996 that saw almost the entire Chinese pro-democracy movement jailed, intimidated into silence or driven into exile.

China rejects international criticisms of its policies on dissent as interference in its internal affairs, arguing that the right to the bare necessities of life is more important than political rights.
